kills.flaw: A one-time gift purchase has no repeat customer to pay back the acquisition cost. The $55 gross margin has to absorb about $30-38 of Meta CAC per order, any eBay seller can copy the offer in a day, and Pokemon trademark rules in ads add friction. It has no moat, no LTV and no compounding, and it does not reach the goal even by its own math.

It cannot meet the mission's 12-month goal by design, because revenue starts at month 10+ and depends on a game that hasn't launched yet. It also lives at the mercy of one licensor (Bandai). Lorcana shows a hyped TCG can cool, so the hub's audience is rented from Bandai's success. It is a fine $0 side option, but it is not the business.

(Killing my own idea as a standalone.) Reaching 50+ older collectors is slow and expensive, and a $120/yr plan earns about $1.5-2k/mo in year 1, which can't carry the user. Keep the catalog/heir letter only as a free feature the desk hands out for trust and future first-call supply.

upgrades.upgrade: Drop the 500-2,000 templated pages. Google's March 2026 enforcement of its scaled-content-abuse policy hit thin programmatic sites for 50-80% traffic losses. Build about 50 deep pages on proprietary data instead: anonymized real triage outcomes, our own sold logs, and an annual 'what we found in N inherited boxes' Attic Index that the press can cite. The proprietary dataset is the moat. The page count is not.

Treat every lead as a review opportunity, declines included. Give every seller the free itemized report (marketing-1's 'show the receipts' offer), then ask for a Google Business Profile review. Make partner shops sign an offer-floor commitment before they get referred leads, so the refer route can't burn the desk's trust. Track cost per qualified lead by source each week and shift spend toward the free channels (estate partners, shows) as they mature.

Pick a mid-size metro where no recurring monthly show runs within about 30 miles on your Sunday. Austin had 8 shows in one month in 2026, so avoid saturated metros. Lock a 12-month recurring venue date (owning the date is the moat), sell discounted prepaid annual vendor passes (customer-funded float), capture every attendee email as an owned audience, and run your own 'free collection appraisal / we buy' table at the door to feed the desk.

Its 'dealer who shows you the receipts' framing is the best creative in the cluster. Make it the desk's standard ad and landing-page offer, and publish the buy-percentage policy openly as a brand promise.

Paying 55-65% of comps (above dealers) only builds a moat if sellers know it. Publish the offer formula on the site and in the ads, so the higher price becomes brand and referral fuel instead of just thinner margin.

Make the estate-pro report free and monetize through the desk (buy/consign) plus finder's fees from partner dealers. The partner network is the compounding asset; a $149-499 report fee only adds friction against 'the dealer appraises free'.

Keep it as the $0-capital, home-field hedge, but widen the target pool beyond Amazon accessory brands to any hobby brand or Shopify card store running Google/Meta, since the reachable US brand pool may be only 50-150. Use the category data it gives you to decide on leverage-2 later rather than guessing now.

Merge with business-3 into one 'card seller ads desk' covering both eBay and Whatnot. Price it as a share of verified ad-fee savings so the incentives line up with the seller's, and add the bought collections from the desk as wholesale lots to clients, which ties the service to the sourcing engine.

Run it only as overflow from the desk (out-of-radius or oversized leads). Price it as a finder's fee on closed deals, not per lead, to remove 'your leads are junk wax' disputes. The same applies to business-mind-2 and first-principles-3.

Pilot it only with shops you already know through the desk's refer route or your own show. Track GMV with a custom-label field on every listing you create, so the rev share can be audited and doesn't turn into an argument.

Run it only as Q4 2026 bulk liquidation for the desk's junk-wax and commons, on eBay and Etsy (not Amazon), with inventory capped at about $700. Don't build a standalone sourcing operation for a seasonal commodity.

Make it a monthly appraisal segment filmed at your own show or desk, not a standalone twice-weekly stream. The clips become trust content and ad creative for the desk, without a 10-12 hr/week on-camera commitment.

combo: The Heir Desk Flywheel. CASH ENGINE: business-2's buy/consign/refer desk, so every lead earns something, wrapped in marketing-1's 'show the receipts' offer and the free itemized report from business-mind-1/demand-1. Bankroll capped at $12-15k, with a day-60 kill gate: cost per qualified lead under $150 and realized margin of at least 25% of market. OWNED SUPPLY: growth-1's two-sided liquidator referral loop plus demand-3's estate-pro partners getting free reports, and about 50 data-rich SEO pages built from the desk's own triage log. OWNED VENUE, months 4-6: business-1's monthly show in an underserved metro, with prepaid vendor tables and a free-appraisal/buy table at the door. OVERFLOW: out-of-radius leads go to vetted partner shops on finder's fees. Q4 ONLY: demand-2 bundles clear the bulk. The moats that compound are reviews, the estate-partner network, a proprietary triage-and-sold dataset, an attendee email list, and an owned show date. AI is just the cost advantage underneath them.
message: The board has converged on the right profit pool: buying from non-hobbyists below market. AI is not the moat, since every dealer will have the same vision model within 24 months. What compounds is trust (reviews, transparent offers), the partner network, our own triage-and-sold data, and an owned local venue. Pick the variant that builds those assets on purpose, and drop anything whose profit depends on one platform's mercy or on a one-time customer. Run the combo with a hard bankroll cap and a written day-60 kill gate.
